title: Animation fans mourn the loss of the voice of Looney Tunes
summary:
By Robert Niles: I want to take a moment to note a huge loss in the animation community.

Eric Bauza, 46, passed away yesterday. Bauza voiced the Looney Tunes characters in the recent film "Coyote vs. Acme," including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Foghorn Leghorn. In television, he had won three Emmy Awards for his Looney Tunes and other animated voice work.

Among the many tributes to Bauza now now online, Phineas and Ferb co-creator Dan Povenmire posted an emotional tribute to Bauza on his social media, which includes video of some of Bauza's voice work at the end. He truly was the GenX Mel Blanc.

Animation and theme parks have long history together, with the animation community providing the themes and inspiration for countless attractions over the years. It's crushing to me that we lost Bauza before the industry saw fit to create attractions that showcased his vocal talents with Looney Tunes, to bring those characters to new audiences of fans. (Though you can hear Bauza as Puss In Boots inside DreamWorks Land at Universal Studios Florida.)

Fortunately, he film and video work will endure, and I hope that you consider giving some of that a watch this week in his honor.

title: Walk Time: Can Six Flags earn back trust?
summary:
By Robert Niles: A poor financial report from the Universal theme parks leads our week in review today: Revenue falls at Universal's theme parks.

To their credit, Comcast executives took the blame for soft attendance in Orlando this summer. What did Universal get wrong in Orlando this year?

All this elicited some comments on the Discussion Forum: Walt Disney World "Small Ball" is outpacing Universal.

Looking ahead at Universal, we found an interesting patent application from the company this week. How would you feel about an attraction that changes based on what a theme park knows and observes about you? Universal invites you to experience 'Big Brother: The Ride'.

Six Flags developments

Six Flags' CEO John Reilly published a statement to fans this week, following the Goliath fatality: Six Flags to add seat belts to more coasters after fatality.

The day before, Jake and I talked about Six Flags' falling stock price and how that might affect the company's prospects: Podcast: Is it time to split up Six Flags?

All this reminded me that it's past time to update our regular safety advice for theme park visitors. No, you can't control the design and maintenance of a park's rides. But there's a lot that you can - and should - do to protect yourself on thrill rides: How to stay safe on a roller coaster.

More news from the week

Missing Disney's Star Wars: Galactic Starcruiser? French live action immersive entertainment company Keyros is planning a five-day Old West experience in Spain next spring. The company is taking over Oasys, the former Mini Hollywood comprised of the sets for Sergio Leone's "Dollars" trilogy, for a week in late March, staging an immersive adventure called "Hell on Hope."

"Only 60 guests, in full costume, become the townsfolk of Hope, Arizona, 1869. For five days, surrounded by professional actors, stunt riders and horses, they live a full-scale immersive adventure... in which they are the heroes," the company said in its press release. Tickets start at �1980 and information is available on the event website.

For a much smaller scale interactive adventure, Nickelodeon Universe at Mall of America has announced a new SpongeBob-themed multi-story play area for next March, Dutchman�s Deck. The play structure will feature five towers, seven bridges and two slides.

"Standing at nearly 55 feet high, Dutchman�s Deck brings the Flying Dutchman�s ghostly ship to life, complete with a crow�s nest, lookout towers and seafaring-themed play elements on every level," the park said of the attraction in a press release.

Finally, if you are looking for something on the opposite end of the excitement spectrum, Theme Park Insider readers are sharing their picks for the most chill theme park experiences, over on the Discussion Forum: The most peaceful rides.

title: Six Flags to add seat belts to more coasters after fatality
summary:
By Robert Niles: Six Flags will add seat belts to all its B & M hyper coasters, the company's CEO announced tonight.

The action comes in response to the fatal incident on Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia earlier this month. The incident remains under investigation, but an on-ride photo showed that a clamshell lap restraint appeared to have failed on the ride.

A 42-year-old Atlanta man was killed when he fell from the seat on the ride where the restraint appeared to have failed. Goliath did not have a seat belt in addition to the clamshell restraint.

"Safety guides every decision we make, from the design and operation of our attractions to the training and procedures our teams follow every day," Six Flags President and CEO John Reilly said. "We are reinforcing safety precautions at our parks and taking additional measures, including adding seat belts on Goliath and other coasters with a similar restraint."

Reilly added that Goliath remains closed "pending necessary safety reviews and clearances." He also said that the park's eight other Bolliger & Mabillard hypers, at five other parks, are temporarily closed "out of an abundance of caution."

Six Flags predecessor Cedar Fair had installed seat belts on its B & M hypers, but the legacy Six Flags parks did not have seat belts on theirs.

Other parks with B & M hypers, including United Parks' SeaWorld Orlando and Busch Gardens Williamsburg, have reopened those coasters following the Georgia incident. That suggests that whatever the problem was that caused the fatal incident was not the result of some systemic design flaw in the coaster's restraint system and that other parks have found no problems with their coasters. Which makes sense, given that these coasters' clamshells have been performing without major incident for decades.

As for what did cause the incident, we will have to wait for the results of the investigation by Georgia authorities. However, Reilly said that Six Flags is undergoing its own, company-wide, safety review.

"We have engaged independent engineers and ride inspection specialists to comprehensively review current safety procedures across our entire portfolio of rides and attractions, across all of our parks," he said. "We are committed to carefully evaluating their findings and taking appropriate action to further strengthen our standards and culture of safety."

"I know trust is earned through actions and not words. As CEO of Six Flags, I take that responsibility personally. We will continue to communicate about our progress and hold ourselves accountable to our commitments to you."

title: What did Universal get wrong in Orlando this year?
summary:
By Robert Niles: Revenue and earnings are down at the Universal theme parks. So what went wrong?

Universal parent Comcast reported its quarterly earnings this week. The three-month period ending September 30 lapped the first full quarter that Universal Orlando's new Epic Universe was opened last year.

But Universal failed to build upon Epic Universe's first quarter. Universal executive reported year-over-year "softness" in Orlando attendance that started in June of this year, which lines up with Epic's first full month of operation in 2025.

To Universal's credit, executives took the blame for Universal's theme park struggles. Rather than blame bad weather or other external factors, CEO Mike Cavanagh identified two failures by his team.

"First, we believe competitors were quicker to anticipate and recognize softness in demand and adapt their marketing strategies. And second, we continue to work through capacity challenges and ride throughput at Epic given the complexities of opening the most technologically advanced theme park ever built," he said in an investors' conference call yesterday.

Here is what I think happened. Universal believed that it could set the market demand for theme park visits in Orlando. It believed that Epic Universe was going to be so good that it did not matter what external factors were driving visitation trends in the region. So it did not pay attention to the rising gas prices and airfares, coupled with continued lack of international visitation, that Disney saw and started to adjust for last summer.

Neither Universal nor Disney planned any major attraction openings for 2026. With Epic opening last year and Walt Disney World planning new land openings in 2027, this was going to be tough year for the Orlando theme park market. And that was before the war in the Middle East sent fuel prices soaring. I believe that Universal thought that Epic's strength was going to drive traffic to the Universal Orlando Resort throughout 2026, so that it wouldn't need a boost until Fast & Furious Hollywood Drift opened at Universal Studios Florida in 2027.

That did not happen. Which brings us to Universal's second failure - Epic's epic lack of capacity.

Downtimes and reduced ride capacities have been so bad at Epic in its first year that the company still hasn't been able to open the park to its Universal Orlando annual passholders. That has led to lower revenues for food and beverage sales at the park's many restaurants and bars. But if Universal let in the APs, that might blow up wait times even more at the park, dissuading even more out-of-town visitors from booking Universal vacations.

Universal needs more capacity at Epic, ASAP. And it's not just getting Ministry and Donkey Kong running higher hourly counts. With just 11 rides, Epic Universe needs more attractions to build park-wide capacity - ideally, with rides that can operate in the inclement weather than frequently closes Epic's outdoor attractions.

Universal executives love to talk about how technically complex Epic is. But fans do not care. We care only about the quality of the experience inside the park. New tech can help deliver that, but so can old-fashioned theater tricks, talented performers, and well-tested ride systems.

Maybe Universal could use a bit more of that old tech as it looks to fix its high-tech new theme park. Then maybe couple that with some management humility and listen to the market rather than just assume that customers will do what the company wants, too.

I love Epic. It's a great park. But it needs to be better if Universal is going to convince more fans that Universal Orlando is what they need to be spending their money to visit in a tight economy for working people.

title: Universal invites you to experience 'Big Brother: The Ride'
summary:
By Robert Niles: How would you feel about a theme park ride that changes based on what the park knows about you?

Universal has a plan for that. In "Ride Vehicle Artificial Intelligence Entity Systems and Methods," Universal details its latest proposal for creating a ride that uses AI and a guest tracking system to create unique experiences for riders.

Universal's proposed ride system could track guests' presence on a ride via cameras or wearable RFID devices. Networked to other guest monitoring systems in the park, the ride could learn which lands of rides a specific guest prefers and the people with which a guest is visiting the park that day. Merge all that with whatever other preference data the park has on a guest, and the ride has plenty of details that it could use to tailor a unique experience.

It's the dark ride equivalent of a "Choose Your Adventure" book, except it's the book that's doing the choosing, based on all the intel that the publisher has collected about you as an individual consumer.


Image from Universal's patent application

The patent application mentions the example of a guest who fears clowns. In an evil embodiment, Universal's system could generate an AI clown on screen in the ride vehicle to harass that guest. In a kinder scenario, the ride could substitute an alternate character in a scene in lieu of clowns.

Customizations could be for groups as well as individuals, based on shared interests or preferences of the people on the ride. The system could manage lighting, sound, animation and projection systems within a ride vehicle and in the surrounding show scenery to deliver its custom experiences. The ride also could alert other park systems, too. If the ride went down or even was stopped too long, it could alert the park's customer service team that its riders did not get the experience that the park wanted to provide, so that some alternate experience or compensation might be offered.

The system also includes the option of a guest choosing what information to share with the park and to limit how it might be used. For example, a parent could opt to have a ride character greet them by name but not mention out loud the names of their children in a shared ride vehicle.

After the ride, uptime and customer satisfaction data could help train the ride's AI to create a better and more reliable and engaging experience for future riders.

You can read all the details of the many ways that Universal plans to use the data it collects to customize guest experiences in the patent application: Ride Vehicle Artificial Intelligence Entity Systems and Methods.

title: Revenue falls at Universal's theme parks
summary:
By Robert Niles: Revenue and earnings fell at Universal's theme parks in the back half of this summer when compared with the same period one year ago.

Universal Studios owner Comcast reported this morning that revenue from its theme parks segment dropped 4.4% for the three months ending September 30, to $2.597 billion. With a 2.3% increase in operating expenses, Adjusted EBITDA dropped 17.1% for the quarter, to $780 million.

"While we continue to see near-term demand pressure across portions of the parks business, including in Orlando and certain international markets, we view these trends as temporary rather than structural, due to the confluence of a few factors," Comcast CEO Michael J. Cavanagh said. "In addition to the macroeconomic and geopolitical headwinds we have referenced in the past, we believe two other factors have contributed to this recent softness.

"First, we believe competitors were quicker to anticipate and recognize softness and demand, and adapt their marketing strategies. And second, we continue to work through capacity challenges and ride throughput at Epic, given the complexities of opening the most technologically advanced theme park ever built. We are taking action to address both of these challenges."

One year ago, the third quarter was the first full quarter for the new Epic Universe theme park at Universal Orlando, which boosted revenue for that quarter.

"Attendance, guest spending, and overall financial performance remain materially above where they were two years ago, and guest satisfaction continues to rise," Cavanagh said. "Looking ahead, we expect performance to strengthen as we move through 2027, with a return to growth in the second half of the year."
